name: Liam Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, which is independent: no AI firms, employers, unions or government involved. Your name won't be attached to anything. Can you take me through an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the small business team at Brindle Commercial, an insurer in the city centre, fourth floor, view of a car park. We cover cafés, hairdressers, corner shops. My day is issuing certificates, setting up new policies from the forms brokers send in, and logging claims when a shop gets broken into or a freezer packs up and all the stock goes off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The good bit is the owners. A guy who runs a kebab shop rang last week because his freezer died, and I got him a payment within four days, and he sent a tray of baklava up for the whole floor. The hard bit is the wording on business policies. There's so much of it, and I still have to ask Sandra, the senior on our team, about half of the odd ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. That's kind of what I expect, if I'm honest. It's a tool, not a miracle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work, well, there we go, back to normal. Online I'd stay out of it, I don't really argue about this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I passed probation in the spring, the small business team's growing because Brindle bought a smaller insurer, and Sandra's been decent about teaching me. If AI just drafts a few emails for me, that's a bonus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, try to get through the wording faster and learn the odd cases myself instead of asking Sandra. I'd use the drafting tool when I remember, like I do now. I'd keep putting a bit by for a car, because the bus to Brindle takes forty minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything at home weighing on you, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Anouk, my girlfriend, is a teaching assistant at a primary school, which is steady. The rent's fine between us. If anything, it's the car, and that's not exactly a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your day would AI take, even in a quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The certificates, I suppose. If the system issued certificates itself, I'd lose an hour a day of the easy stuff, but I'd just have more claims to log. The claims team are always behind anyway.

say: At work I'd say **back to normal**, it's a tool, not a miracle.
I'd **stay out of** online arguments about AI, because I don't argue about this stuff.
think: I passed **probation** and the team's growing, so I'd be fine.
If AI takes **certificates**, I'd just log more claims.
do: Learn **odd policy wording** myself instead of asking the senior.
Use the **drafting tool** when I remember, like now.
Keep saving for **a car** to cut the forty-minute bus.
S0.quote: If the system issued certificates itself, I'd lose an hour a day of the easy stuff, but I'd just have more claims to log.
fieldNote: He's **secure enough**: a growing team, passed probation, and a partner in steady work.
He sees AI as **a tool**, not a miracle, and it shows.
The **car savings** goal is the only money pressure he names.

steps.text: Learn odd business policy wording without asking Sandra
Save each month towards a car for the commute

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's more likely than people think. Brokers are already sending us forms that a machine filled in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, look, things change, we'll adapt. I'd probably say it at five-a-side as well, because a couple of the lads work in offices too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think our team gets smaller. Setting up policies from forms, checking them, logging claims, that's all on your list. I'm junior and I'm not the fastest. If Brindle cut two out of eight on our team, I could easily be one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI drafting and checking tools properly, every day, once the others had shown it works. I'd ask Sandra what the people who stay would be doing, probably the complicated claims and talking to owners. I'd also push the savings from about three months to five, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sick in the stomach. Like before a review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start looking for another job straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nah, not yet. I'd want to see if my team actually gets cut first. If it starts happening, then I'd look, and I'd look at broker jobs, where you're on the phone with shop owners all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of the job would you hang on to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The baklava guy, honestly. People like him want to talk to someone. I think that's where I'd try to stay, on the side where you talk to people.

say: I'd say **things change** and we'll adapt.
I'd say the same at **five-a-side** to mates in office jobs.
think: Our **team gets smaller**, because forms, checks and claims are on the list.
I'm junior and slow, so if two of eight go, **I could be one**.
do: Use the **AI tools daily** once colleagues show they work.
Ask the senior what the **remaining roles** will be.
Push savings from **three to five months**.
feel: **Sick in the stomach**, like before a review.
S1.quote: If Brindle cut two out of eight on our team, I could easily be one.
fieldNote: He's **pragmatic**: waits for proof, then commits to the tools.
He'd stay on the **people-facing** side of insurance, where owners want a voice.
He's composed, but expects a **real chance** of being cut.

steps.text: Use the AI drafting and checking tools every working day
Lift savings from three months to five months
Look at broker jobs if Brindle starts cutting the team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, it's too fast, and somebody in charge needs to slow it down. I'm not political, but I'd vote for whoever had an actual plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it finishes my job. Brindle would run the whole small business book with a couple of people checking the machine. A junior like me isn't one of those people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at jobs where you're on your feet with people, straight away. My brother-in-law does shop fitting, and he's always short of hands. I'd keep my Brindle job as long as it lasted, save hard, forget the car, and start doing Saturdays with him to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly scared, more than I'd let on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots come about three years later. What does that do to your shop-fitting idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's the thing that'd keep me up. Shop fitting would only last about three years past the AI, so I'd be retraining twice, which is exhausting just to think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean for your girlfriend's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. Anouk's school might be safer, because kids need people in the room. So she'd probably be the steady one, and I'd be the one changing jobs every few years.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and someone needs to slow it down.
I'd vote for **whoever had a plan**, though I'm not political.
think: It **finishes my job**; Brindle would run the book with a few checkers.
Shop fitting buys about **three years**, then I'd retrain again.
do: Start **Saturday shifts** with my brother-in-law's shop-fitting business.
**Save hard** and drop the car plan.
Vote for the **party with a plan** for workers.
feel: **Properly scared**, more than I'd let on.
S2.quote: Shop fitting would only last about three years past the AI, so I'd be retraining twice, which is exhausting just to think about.
fieldNote: He used the **three-year gap** to see a trade as a stopgap, not a fix.
His girlfriend's **school job** becomes the household anchor.
His **centre outlook** shows: he votes for a plan, not a side.

steps.text: Work Saturdays with his brother-in-law's shop-fitting firm
Drop the car plan and bank the money instead
Vote for whichever party has a real plan for workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's still fast, but it's workable, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, but not loads, so people should start planning. I'd say it to the lads, and to my sister, who's still at college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still expect Brindle to go mostly AI by the end. But five years means I could move sideways while I'm still employed, instead of jumping after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Brindle about moving into the loss adjuster side. Loss adjusters go out and look at the damage in the shop. That's half hands-on, so the job lasts longer. I'd do their training course in year one, keep saving, and maybe get the car after all, because adjusters need one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. But like I've got a steering wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for proof before. Would you move earlier this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair, but I'd want to see others go first. Sandra says two people on the claims team already moved into adjusting, and they like it. If it works for them, I'd follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put on hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably moving in with Anouk properly, getting a bigger place. We'd hold off on that while I sorted the job.

say: I'd say there's **time, but not loads**, so start planning.
I'd tell my **younger sister** at college to plan ahead.
think: Brindle goes **mostly AI** by the end anyway.
Five years means I can **move sideways** while still employed.
do: Ask Brindle to move into **loss adjusting**, which is half hands-on.
Take their **adjuster training** in year one.
Hold off on a **bigger flat** with my girlfriend until the job's sorted.
feel: **Nervous**, but like I've got a steering wheel.
S3.quote: Loss adjusters go out and look at the damage in the shop. That's half hands-on, so the job lasts longer.
fieldNote: He found a **sideways move** inside insurance that adds hands-on time.
He still needs **colleagues to go first** before he commits.
A **bigger flat** is the plan he'd pause.

steps.text: Ask Brindle to move into loss adjusting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Yeah, okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off, there's time for everyone to get ready. I'd also say, don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay at Brindle for a while and get good, then move into adjusting or broking around thirty-two. I'd have time to do it in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more each year, because by then they'd be everywhere. I'd get the car, move in with Anouk properly, and do the adjuster course in year three or four. I'd want around six months saved by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little uneasy, because I know I'd be tempted to put things off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about having children in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, maybe. Anouk would want to. Ten years is enough to have a kid and still sort the job out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years take the worry away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not more than I'd get anyway. The worry is still there. It's just not right in front of me.

say: I'd say it's a long way off and there's **time for everyone** to get ready.
I'd also tell people **don't waste it**, because ten years goes quickly.
think: I'd **stay at Brindle** for a while and get properly good at the job first.
Around **thirty-two** I'd move into adjusting or broking, doing things in the right order.
do: Use the **AI tools more** each year as they spread.
Do the **adjuster course** in year three or four.
**Move in properly** with my girlfriend and think about a child.
feel: Mostly calm, a little **uneasy** about putting things off.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to have a kid and still sort the job out.
fieldNote: With a decade, he plans in **the right order**: skill, then move.
**Children** come up for the first time once pressure eases.

steps.text: Use the AI tools at Brindle a bit more each year
Do the loss adjuster course in year three or four
Move in properly with Anouk and plan a first child

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be retraining twice in five years. What would help is companies telling us early what's being automated and moving people sideways before they cut. Even six months' notice would make a difference.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what customers want. The shop owners I talk to don't want to argue with a chatbot when their stock's ruined. I think that matters more than people at the top think.

headlineQuote: The shop owners I talk to don't want to argue with a chatbot when their stock's ruined.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old** small business insurance clerk at Brindle Commercial, still learning policy wording.
He lives with his girlfriend, a **teaching assistant**, and is saving for a car.
He's **pragmatic**: he waits for proof, then commits to tools or moves.
As scenarios speed up, he looks to **shop fitting** and later loss adjusting for more hands-on time.
He believes customers want a **real person** when things go wrong.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have to retrain twice in a few years.
whatWouldHelp: **Early warning** of automation and sideways moves before any cuts.
